name: Walther P38 (Pistole 38)
feed: 8-round detachable single-stack box magazine
action: Short recoil with hinged locking piece; double-action/single-action

variants.name: Zero series (0-prefix serials)
variants.notes: Three prototype/test series; mass production began mid-1940 under Walther code 480.

variants.name: ac (Walther, Zella-Mehlis)
variants.notes: Marked ac + year, e.g. ac43. 617,585 made in WWII.

variants.name: byf (Mauser, Oberndorf)
variants.notes: Marked byf + year. 372,875 made. Start date not verified.

variants.name: cyq / cvq (Spreewerk, Grottau)
variants.notes: No date stamps. 287,220 made. Late-war die broke: about 31,400 marked cvq.

variants.name: svw (Mauser 1945) and postwar 'grey ghost'
variants.notes: OUT OF PERIOD. 1945 Mauser code; French occupation assembly 1945-46 marked svw46, parkerized, sheet-metal grips.

variants.name: Grip material
variants.notes: Early walnut grips, later Bakelite.

variants.name: 7.65mm Parabellum P38
variants.notes: Small numbers from 1943.

reliability_notes: No systemic problem documented in the sources checked. Comment-section claims of cracked slides or frames are unverified. Muzzle velocity figure is flagged as needing a citation on Wikipedia.

name: Luger P08 (Pistole 08 / Parabellum)
feed: 8-round detachable box magazine (LP 08: 32-round Trommelmagazin 08 snail drum)

variants.name: P08
variants.notes: 100 mm barrel. Muzzle velocity 350-400 m/s (range in source; JSON uses midpoint).

variants.name: LP 08 Artillery
variants.notes: 200 mm barrel, 8-position tangent sight, shoulder stock, snail drum.

variants.name: Pistole 04 (Navy)
variants.notes: 150 mm barrel, two-position sight. Relevant to Kriegsmarine bases in Brittany.

variants.name: Krieghoff Luftwaffe contract
variants.notes: From 1935; second contract of 15,000 unfinished when Krieghoff stopped in 1944.

variants.name: Mauser production
variants.notes: Rust blue and straw-finished small parts dropped in the 1930s; black Bakelite grips on some from 1941; P08 production ended December 1943. Factory codes S/42, 42, byf inferred from the Mauser Oberndorf code list.

reliability_notes: Sensitive to ammunition: low-pressure loads may not cycle the toggle. Wikipedia describes above-average mud resistance, so the 'jams when dirty' reputation is not supported; poorly assembled or salvaged guns are blamed for much of its bad name.

name: Walther PP
feed: 8-round detachable box magazine (.32 ACP; 7 in .380)

variants.name: .32 ACP
variants.notes: Most common service chambering; 320 m/s (Wikipedia flags as needing citation).

variants.name: .380 ACP / 9mm Kurz
variants.notes: 7 rounds, 256 m/s, 665 g.

variants.name: .22 LR
variants.notes: 10 rounds; training and sporting.

reliability_notes: No problems documented in sources checked. Late-war finish changes not found.

name: Walther PPK
feed: 7-round detachable box magazine (.32 ACP; 6 in .380)

variants.name: .32 ACP
variants.notes: 7 rounds.

variants.name: .380 ACP
variants.notes: 6 rounds.

reliability_notes: No problems documented. Issued to Ordnungspolizei, Kriminalpolizei detectives, party officials and officers; Gestapo use is an inference, not stated in the source.

name: Mauser HSc
feed: 8-round detachable box magazine (.380: 7)

variants.name: Early Army/Navy pistols
variants.notes: Highly polished, richly blued, wood grips. Wartime split 1940-45: Heer 137,121, Polizei 28,300, Kriegsmarine 27,100, commercial 59,467.

variants.name: 3rd/4th Army variations
variants.notes: Finish declines, rougher polish, sight-channel machining removed.

variants.name: Late (#940,000+)
variants.notes: Some black plastic grips; final pistols (about #949,500-952,000) phosphate finish.

reliability_notes: No problems documented in sources checked.

name: Sauer 38H
feed: 8-round detachable box magazine
action: Straight blowback, double-action with cocking/decocking lever

variants.name: Standard wartime
variants.notes: About 200,000 made 1938-45; mainly Luftwaffe and police.

variants.name: Late-war simplified
variants.notes: Rougher finish, simpler markings, no slide safety, some without decocking lever. Final April 1945 guns out of period.

reliability_notes: Late simplified examples described as still fully functional.

name: FN Browning Model 1910 / Model 1922 (German police issue)
feed: Detachable box magazine (M1922: 9 x .32 / 8 x .380; M1910: 7 x .32 / 6 x .380)

variants.name: Model 1910
variants.notes: About 590 g, 80 mm barrel.

variants.name: Model 1922
variants.notes: About 700 g, 113 mm barrel; produced at occupied FN for German police use.

reliability_notes: No problems documented in sources checked. German designations Pistole 626(b)/641(b) appear in lists but model mapping not confirmed.

name: Radom Vis wz. 35 (Pistole P 35(p))
feed: 8-round detachable box magazine

variants.name: Polish pre-war
variants.notes: High quality; about 49,400 delivered before September 1939.

variants.name: German series 1-4
variants.notes: About 375,000 for the Heer (Hogg estimate); progressively simplified; final series marked only bnz (Steyr). All-Steyr production from late 1944 is out of period.

reliability_notes: German wartime pistols described as 'much lower quality' than Polish originals, declining further late in the war.

name: CZ vz. 27 (Pistole 27(t))
feed: 9-round detachable box magazine

variants.name: Occupation production (fnh)
variants.notes: Slide marked fnh, German code for Ceska Zbrojovka Strakonice; Heer issue.

reliability_notes: No problems documented; late-war quality changes not found.

name: Browning Hi-Power (Pistole 640(b))
feed: 13-round double-stack detachable box magazine

variants.name: FN under German occupation
variants.notes: Over 300,000 for the Wehrmacht, German acceptance marks (e.g. WaA613); mainly Waffen-SS and Fallschirmjäger.

variants.name: Inglis (Canada)
variants.notes: OUT OF PERIOD: Allied production began late 1944.

reliability_notes: Stories of Belgian worker sabotage and degraded wartime quality were not confirmed in sources checked.

name: Mauser C96 (and M712 Schnellfeuer)
feed: 10-round fixed internal magazine loaded by stripper clip (M712: 10/20-round detachable box)

variants.name: C96 / M1930
variants.notes: Semi-auto; Heer received 19,000 in 1942, Luftwaffe about 7,800-8,000. Effective range 150-200 m (JSON midpoint). 9mm version 350 m/s.

variants.name: M712 Schnellfeuer (M1932)
variants.notes: Fully automatic, 900-1,000 rpm; small numbers to the Wehrmacht.

variants.name: Stock holster
variants.notes: Wooden holster attaches as a shoulder stock.

reliability_notes: No specific problems documented in sources checked. Automatic M712 is very hard to control (inferred from rate of fire).

name: Karabiner 98k
feed: Internal 5-round box; 5-round stripper clip or single rounds

variants.name: Pre-1937 numeric codes
variants.notes: 27 Erma, 42 Mauser Oberndorf (S/42), 147 Sauer, 237 BLM, 243 Mauser Borsigwalde, 337 Gustloff, 660 Steyr, 945 Brno.

variants.name: Letter codes from 1937
variants.notes: ar Mauser Borsigwalde, ax Erma, bcd Gustloff, bnz Steyr, byf Mauser Oberndorf, ce Sauer, dot Brno, dou Bystrica, duv BLM. svw45/swp45 are 1945, out of period.

variants.name: Stock and finish
variants.notes: Laminated stocks from 1937 (stronger, resist warping); phosphate finish from 1944.

variants.name: Kriegsmodell
variants.notes: OUT OF PERIOD: from late 1944; no bayonet lug, cleaning rod or stock disc; stamped bands.

variants.name: Sniper (ZF39 4x / ZF41 1.5x)
variants.notes: About 132,000 sniper rifles; ZF39 for head/chest shots to 400 m; ZF41 from 1941 (100,000+). Scoped effective range 800-1,000 m.

variants.name: Schiessbecher grenade launcher
variants.notes: 30 mm cup launcher from 1942, effective to 280 m; 1,450,113 made.

reliability_notes: No systemic problems documented. Weight 3.7-4.1 kg in source (JSON midpoint).

name: Gewehr 43 (G43)
feed: 10-round detachable box magazine; can be topped up with 5-round stripper clips
action: Gas-operated short-stroke piston, flapper locking, semi-automatic

variants.name: G43
variants.notes: Production began October 1943. Muzzle velocity 746-776 m/s depending on source (JSON midpoint).

variants.name: K43
variants.notes: OUT OF PERIOD as a name: renamed April 1944.

variants.name: ZF4 scoped
variants.notes: About 50,000-53,435 sniper rifles; 4x, range drum 100-800 m; effective 800 m.

variants.name: Maker codes
variants.notes: ac Walther, duv then qve BLM, bcd Gustloff.

reliability_notes: More reliable than the fouling-prone G41. Planned issue of 19 per company was never achieved; with production only from October 1943, it is near-absent in Brittany in winter 1943-44.

name: MP 40 (and MP 38)
feed: 32-round double-column single-feed detachable box magazine (service practice: 28 rounds)
action: Open-bolt straight blowback, fully automatic only

variants.name: MP 38
variants.notes: Machined receiver with grooves, round hole in magazine housing, 4.2 kg. Early guns could not lock the bolt.

variants.name: MP 38/40 conversion
variants.notes: Bolt-locking safety notch standard from 1941 and retrofitted.

variants.name: MP 40
variants.notes: Stamped and spot-welded; ribbed magazine housing; ribbed magazines from 1941. About 1.05-1.1 million made by Erma, Haenel and Steyr (bnz). Codes ayf (Erma) and fxo (Haenel) are commonly cited but unverified.

variants.name: MP 40/I
variants.notes: Experimental dual-magazine version, late 1942; very rare.

reliability_notes: Magazine is the weak point: friction where the columns merge, dirt, and gripping the magazine misaligns it. Folding stock not always durable. Early MP 38s could fire if knocked. Rate 500-550 rpm, effective range 100-200 m (JSON midpoints).

name: MG 34 (enemy emplacement)
feed: 50-round belts (linkable to 250), 50-round Gurttrommel belt drum, or rare 75-round saddle drum
action: Recoil-operated, open bolt, rotating bolt, muzzle booster

variants.name: Standard
variants.notes: 800-900 rpm (JSON midpoint); 32 kg on tripod. Effective 200-2,000 m with sight adjustments (JSON midpoint); 3,500 m on tripod with optic.

variants.name: MG 34S / MG 34/41
variants.notes: Higher-rate experimental/limited variants (1,500 and about 1,200 rpm).

variants.name: Panzerlauf
variants.notes: Armoured barrel jacket for vehicles; about 50,000 made.

reliability_notes: Sensitive to extreme weather, dirt and mud; tight tolerances. Recommend enemy-only (weight, belts).

name: MG 42 (enemy emplacement)
feed: 50/250-round belts or 50-round belt drum

variants.name: Standard
variants.notes: About 1,200 rpm cyclic (900-1,500 with different bolts); barrel change in under 10 s. First combat May 1942; 116,725 made in 1943. Effective 200-2,000 m (JSON midpoint).

reliability_notes: No specific issues documented. Static coastal divisions likely held more MG 34s and captured MGs than MG 42s (inference). Recommend enemy-only.

name: Leuchtpistole 34 / Leuchtpistole 42 (flare pistol)
feed: Single cartridge; break-open, manually loaded

variants.name: Leuchtpistole 34
variants.notes: Walther (also Erma, Berhauss); duralumin frame, steel barrel, Bakelite grips; 245 mm; introduced 1934.

variants.name: Leuchtpistole 42
variants.notes: Stamped galvanised mild steel; introduced 1943 per German Wikipedia.

variants.name: Kampfpistole / Sturmpistole
variants.notes: Rifled 'Z' version firing grenades: Panzerwurfkörper 42 HEAT (69 m, 80 mm penetration), Wurfgranate 326, Wurfkörper 361.

variants.name: Ammunition
variants.notes: Single and multi-star signals, parachute illumination, smoke.

reliability_notes: No issues documented. Firing a flare should reveal the player to every patrol in sight.

name: MAS-36 (German Gewehr 242(f))
feed: Internal 5-round box loaded by 5-round stripper clips

variants.name: French Army
variants.notes: Made from late 1937; only 250,000 available in 1940. Spike bayonet stored reversed under barrel.

variants.name: Gewehr 242(f)
variants.notes: Captured rifles issued to German occupation units in France.

reliability_notes: No manual safety (typical of French rifles of the period).

name: Lebel Mle 1886/M93 (German Gewehr 301(f))
feed: 8-round tube magazine under the barrel, loaded one round at a time (+1 on elevator, +1 in chamber = 10 total)
action: Bolt action, two front locking lugs

variants.name: Mle 1886/M93
variants.notes: 1893 bolt-head change vents burst-case gas away from the face. Muzzle velocity 610-700 m/s (JSON midpoint); Balle D 730 m/s per cartridge article.

variants.name: M93-R35 carbine
variants.notes: About 45 cm barrel, 3-round tube; about 50,000 assembled from 1937.

variants.name: Gewehr 301(f)
variants.notes: Issued in limited numbers to occupation troops in 1944.

reliability_notes: Slow tube-magazine reload is its 'worst handicap'. No safety, so carrying chambered is unsafe. Primer groove and cap stop spitzer tips setting off rounds in the tube.

name: Berthier Mousqueton Mle 1892/M16 and Fusil 1907/15 (German K 553(f) / G 304(f) / G 241(f))
feed: Mannlicher-type en-bloc clip (3-round early, 5-round M16); empty clip drops out of the bottom

variants.name: Mousqueton Mle 1892/M16
variants.notes: 5-round carbine, 3.25 kg, 637 m/s. German Karabiner 553(f); captured carbines issued to Atlantic Wall units.

variants.name: Fusil Mle 1907/15
variants.notes: 3-round, 3.81 kg; 435,000 made.

variants.name: Fusil Mle 1907/15-M16
variants.notes: 5-round, 4.195 kg; German Gewehr 304(f).

variants.name: Mle 1907/15-M34
variants.notes: 7.5×54mm, 850 m/s, 3.7 kg; about 80,000 converted; German Gewehr 241(f).

reliability_notes: No mechanical safety. M16 guns have a spring trapdoor to keep mud out of the clip opening. Topping off with loose rounds is not documented; suggest a clips-only reload rule.

name: Pistolet automatique Modèle 1935A (German Pistole 625(f))
feed: 8-round detachable box magazine

variants.name: French pre-occupation
variants.notes: About 10,700 made by SACM before summer 1940.

variants.name: Pistole 625(f)
variants.notes: About 23,850 made for German forces under occupation.

reliability_notes: 7.65 Longue is a weak cartridge; surplus French ammo is described today as scarce, corrosive and unreliable.

name: Pistolet automatique Modèle 1935S
feed: 8-round detachable box magazine

variants.name: MAS 1940
variants.notes: Only about 1,404 made when Saint-Étienne was occupied. Source also gives MAS 6,686 cumulative by late 1944, which conflicts with 'not produced during the occupation'.

variants.name: ManuFrance / SAGEM / MAC
variants.notes: 1944-56 production, mostly out of period.

reliability_notes: Same weak 7.65 Longue cartridge as the 1935A.

name: MAB Model D
feed: 9-round detachable box magazine (.380: 7)

variants.name: Civil / French
variants.notes: Made from 1933.

variants.name: German-accepted
variants.notes: Adopted by the Wehrmacht during the occupation; German acceptance marks (fakes common on collector pieces).

reliability_notes: No problems documented. Muzzle velocity as published (low for .32 ACP).

name: Ruby-type 'Eibar' pistol (German Pistole 624(f))
feed: 9-round detachable box magazine (often not interchangeable between makers)

variants.name: Gabilondo Ruby
variants.notes: 250,000-300,000 of the original maker.

variants.name: Subcontractor Ruby-types
variants.notes: France accepted about 710,000 from all sources; about 580,000 still in army stores in 1920. Quality varies widely.

variants.name: Pistole 624(f)
variants.notes: German designation; Germans also continued an external-hammer version.

reliability_notes: Poor finish and incorrectly hardened steel on many could cause a dangerous 'runaway gun'; some had faulty safeties. Magazines rarely interchange, so French magazine bases were marked. Good examples reliable and accurate.

name: Modèle 1892 revolver ('Lebel revolver')
feed: 6-shot cylinder swinging out to the right; loaded one round at a time

variants.name: Mle 1892
variants.notes: Over 350,000 made 1892-1924; police until mid-1960s and Gendarmerie.

reliability_notes: No problems documented. Its cartridge is unique in the roster (no other gun takes it).

name: MAS-38 (German MP 722(f))
feed: 32-round detachable box magazine
action: Blowback, bolt travelling at an angle to the bore, automatic

variants.name: French 1939-40
variants.notes: Fewer than 1,000 delivered by June 1940 (Forgotten Weapons) or 1,958 made before occupation (Wikipedia).

variants.name: MP 722(f)
variants.notes: 20-30 thousand made under German control (Forgotten Weapons); some to Vichy forces.

reliability_notes: High-quality, machined from solid steel, controllable; weak cartridge (roughly 9×18mm Makarov class). Rate 600-700 rpm (JSON midpoint). Safety locks the bolt when the trigger is pushed forward.

name: Manufrance Robust (double-barrel hunting shotgun)
feed: Break-open, two barrels, shells loaded singly (paper hulls in period)
action: Anson & Deeley boxlock, two triggers, top lever, cocked on opening

variants.name: Robust (1913)
variants.notes: 12 and 16 gauge; 70-80 cm barrels; nearly 900,000 made overall; the reference French shotgun, used by FFI and FTP. Weight 2.8-3.2 kg from later variants (JSON midpoint).

variants.name: Manufrance Idéal (1887)
variants.notes: Earlier double-barrel hunting gun.

variants.name: Manufrance Simplex (1908)
variants.notes: Introduced 1908; details not found.

variants.name: Out of period
variants.notes: Rapid pump (1958) and Perfex semi-auto (1962).

reliability_notes: Effective range with lead shot depends on choke: 18 m cylinder to 37 m full (JSON midpoint); slugs about 100 m. Hunting arms banned by German ordinance of 5 March 1942, so every one is hidden. Paper-shell swelling in damp is plausible but unsourced.

name: Sten Mk II (and Mk I/Mk III family)
feed: 32-round double-column single-feed side-mounted box magazine (loading tool issued; interchangeable with Lanchester magazines)

variants.name: Mk I / Mk I*
variants.notes: About 100,000; wooden furniture, flash hider on Mk I.

variants.name: Mk II
variants.notes: Contracts August 1941; removable barrel, rotating magazine housing; about 2-2.6 million made. Breaks into four parts for hiding.

variants.name: Mk II (Canadian, Long Branch)
variants.notes: Skeleton stock, 3.8 kg.

variants.name: Mk III
variants.notes: Lines Bros only, 876,794 by September 1943; fixed barrel; Mk II judged superior. Reader claim of loose barrel shifting point of impact unverified.

variants.name: Mk V
variants.notes: OUT OF PERIOD: designed 1943, first combat June 1944.

reliability_notes: Bent magazine lips (precise 8-degree feed angle) and dirt in the magazine taper cause misfeeds; gripping the magazine causes stoppages. A loaded Sten could fire by accident if dropped or knocked butt-first on the ground (the bolt can pick up and fire a round). Quality varied by maker. Heavy carbon can stop the firing pin. Rate 500-600 rpm (JSON midpoint). Does NOT take MP 40 magazines (unsupported claim).

name: Sten Mk II(S) (suppressed)
feed: 32-round double-column single-feed side-mounted box magazine
action: Open-bolt blowback, select fire (instructions: single shots only)

variants.name: Mk II(S)
variants.notes: Requested 1942, trials November 1942, production pattern adopted February 1944; 5,776 made. 3.75 in ported barrel, about 12 in integral suppressor with expansion chamber and 18 baffles; bolt lightened about 15%.

reliability_notes: Automatic fire could compress and damage the baffles (Forgotten Weapons); Wikipedia says it overheats fast, so it was fired in short bursts or singles, with a canvas cover for the hand, and some were converted to semi-only. Open-bolt clatter is unsuppressed; reader reports of occasional sonic crack. Rate of fire and weight not found. Effective range up to 100 m (German Wikipedia).

name: Welrod Mk II / Mk IIA (and 9mm Mk I)
caliber: .32 ACP (7.65×17mm) for Mk II/IIA; 9×19mm for 9mm Mk I
feed: Detachable magazine forming the grip (8 x .32 / 6 x 9mm per English Wikipedia; 5 per German Wikipedia)
action: Manually operated rotating bolt (turn rear knob, pull, push, lock)

variants.name: Mk I prototype (.32)
variants.notes: Concept January 1943, samples April 1943; fixed 5-round magazine, thumb trigger; 'rather awkward'.

variants.name: Mk II / Mk IIA (.32 ACP)
variants.notes: Developed June 1943, adopted after trials; the main wartime model. About 2,800 Welrods made in wartime.

variants.name: 9mm Mk I
variants.notes: Developed after poor field results with .32; has a trigger guard.

reliability_notes: Rubber wipes degrade fast: about 15 shots before performance declines quickly; in a 2024 test it went from a muffled thump to a gunshot-like crack over about 8 shots after the front wipe holed. Effective range 23 m by day, 6-7 m at night (12-15 m per German Wikipedia). Documented use mostly Danish; German Wikipedia names France among countries of use.

name: Colt M1911 / M1911A1
feed: 7-round detachable single-stack box magazine

variants.name: M1911
variants.notes: Adopted 1911.

variants.name: M1911A1
variants.notes: Changes completed 1924, designated 1926: shorter trigger, arched mainspring housing, longer grip-safety spur, wider front sight. WWII makers Remington Rand, Colt, Ithaca, Union Switch & Signal, Singer (about 1.9 million).

reliability_notes: No problems documented. Wikipedia says SOE 'prized' the M1911A1, and SOE used US pistols from 1941; no France-specific numbers found.

name: Colt Model 1903 Pocket Hammerless
feed: 8-round detachable box magazine

variants.name: M1903 (.32)
variants.notes: Thousands to Britain via Lend-Lease; 20,000 M1903/1908 issued to US specialist personnel including OSS.

variants.name: SOE remote-fire conversion
variants.notes: Strapped to the waist and fired by remote trigger (Forgotten Weapons book review).

reliability_notes: The popular claim that SOE agents routinely carried Colt .32s was not confirmed in sources checked.

name: Webley Mk IV (.38/200)
feed: 6-shot cylinder; top-break with simultaneous extraction of all cases

variants.name: Mk IV .38/200
variants.notes: About 500,000 made; widely issued in WWII because Enfield could not make enough No. 2s.

variants.name: Mk VI .455
variants.notes: WWI revolver, 1.1 kg, 190 m/s, still widely used in WWII.

reliability_notes: No problems documented. SOE issue not stated in source; presence in drops inferred from 57,849 pistols of unknown types delivered to France.

name: Enfield No. 2 Mk I / Mk I* / Mk I**
feed: 6-shot cylinder; top-break with automatic ejection of all cases
action: Mk I double/single action; Mk I* and Mk I** double-action only

variants.name: Mk I
variants.notes: Adopted 1931; about 55,000.

variants.name: Mk I*
variants.notes: 1938; spurless hammer, double-action only, lighter pull.

variants.name: Mk I**
variants.notes: 1942 simplified wartime version, soon discontinued. Mk I*/** together about 270,000.

reliability_notes: Double-action-only pull limits accuracy beyond about 15 yd (13.7 m). Very fast to reload.

name: Smith & Wesson .38/200 British Service Revolver / Victory Model
feed: 6-shot swing-out cylinder, single-round loading

variants.name: British Service Revolver
variants.notes: Mostly 4 or 5 in barrels to Britain; 5 in standard after 4 April 1942.

variants.name: Victory Model
variants.notes: V-prefix serials, sandblasted and parkerized, 1942-44; 590,305 to the Commonwealth in .38/200.

reliability_notes: No problems documented. OSS supplied thousands to resistance forces (timing and France not specified).

name: Lee-Enfield (SMLE No. 1 Mk III/III*, Rifle No. 4 Mk I)
feed: 10-round detachable box magazine, loaded from 5-round chargers

variants.name: SMLE No. 1 Mk III / Mk III*
variants.notes: Mk III 1907, Mk III* late 1915; 3.96 kg.

variants.name: Rifle No. 4 Mk I / Mk I*
variants.notes: Adopted 1941; 4.11 kg; Mk I* made by Long Branch (Canada) and Stevens-Savage (US).

reliability_notes: No problems documented. 127,330 rifles of unspecified type were delivered to France in SOE containers over the whole war.

name: Bren Mk I / Mk II
feed: 30-round top-mounted curved box (loaded with 27-28 to avoid jams; 20 if stored loaded long-term); 100-round pan available

variants.name: Mk I
variants.notes: Drum rear sight, buttstrap, rear grip, telescoping bipod.

variants.name: Mk II (1941)
variants.notes: Simplified, 20-25% cheaper; leaf sight, fixed bipod, slightly higher rate. Inglis (Canada) built 186,000 of all variants.

reliability_notes: 'By general consent the finest light machine gun... of its period'; the maquis begged for more. 20,518 delivered to France over the war, mostly after D-Day. Rate 500-520 rpm (JSON midpoint).

name: Thompson M1928A1 / M1 / M1A1
feed: 20- or 30-round box magazine; 50-round L drum (M1928A1 only)
action: Select fire (M1928A1 delayed blowback; M1/M1A1 straight blowback)

variants.name: M1928A1
variants.notes: Takes drums; 600-725 rpm (JSON midpoint); 4.9 kg; 562,511 made. France had some in 1940 as 'PM 11mm43 M.28 A1'.

variants.name: M1 / M1A1
variants.notes: 1942; box magazines only; M1A1 700-800 rpm, 4.5 kg.

reliability_notes: British found the drum heavy and noisy. Drops to France not documented in sources checked; a hidden 1940 French gun is the most defensible way in.

name: FP-45 Liberator
feed: Single shot, loaded by hand; empty case knocked out with the supplied wooden dowel; 10 spare rounds stored in the grip

variants.name: FP-45
variants.notes: 1,000,000 made June-August 1942 by GM Guide Lamp; shipped with 10 rounds and a wordless comic-strip instruction sheet.

reliability_notes: Crude, smoothbore-class accuracy; effective range 7.3-7.6 m (two figures in source; JSON midpoint). French use undocumented: one German policeman claimed thousands circulated in France; fewer than 25,000 of about 500,000 shipped to Britain were authorised for distribution. Arguably absent.
